title: LEFT and RIGHT JOINs: Keeping All Records 🧾
description: Retain all rows from one table even if there’s no match in the other with LEFT/RIGHT JOIN.

slides.title: LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN) ⬅️
slides.content:
# Keep All Rows from the Left Table

`LEFT JOIN` returns all rows from the left table (the first one), and matching rows from the right table. If no match, NULLs appear for right‑table columns.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Every customer appears, even those with no orders.

slides.title: LEFT JOIN Example
slides.content: Run this on our sample data:
slides.codeSnippet:
SELECT c.name, o.order_id, o.amount
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
ORDER BY c.name;

slides.title: Result Explanation 📋
slides.content:
```
name    | order_id | amount
--------|----------|-------
Alice   | 101      | 250
Alice   | 103      | 320
Bob     | 102      | 180
Charlie | NULL     | NULL
```

Charlie appears with NULLs because he has no orders. This is useful for finding customers who haven’t ordered.

quizData.question: What does LEFT JOIN guarantee?

options.text: All rows from the right table appear
All rows from the left table appear

quizData.explanation: LEFT JOIN preserves every row of the left table.

slides.title: Finding Unmatched Rows 🔍
slides.content:
## Who has no orders?

Add a `WHERE` clause checking for NULL in a column from the right table:

```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;
```

This returns customers who never placed an order.

slides.title: Unmatched Example
slides.codeSnippet: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

slides.title: RIGHT JOIN (RIGHT OUTER JOIN) ➡️
slides.content:
# Keep All Rows from the Right Table

`RIGHT JOIN` is the opposite: all rows from the right table appear, with NULLs for missing left‑table matches.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.order_id
FROM customers c
RIGHT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;
```

Here, order 104 (customer_id=4) appears with NULL customer name.

Note: Many developers avoid RIGHT JOIN by simply swapping the table order and using LEFT JOIN. It’s equivalent.

slides.title: RIGHT JOIN Example
slides.content: All orders, with customer info if available:

quizData.question: If you swap the tables and use LEFT JOIN instead of RIGHT JOIN, will the results be the same?

options.text: Yes, if you also swap the column references
Only if there are no NULLs

quizData.explanation: `A RIGHT JOIN B` = `B LEFT JOIN A`. Swapping and using LEFT yields identical rows, just column order might differ.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Stick with LEFT JOIN

For consistency and readability, most SQL developers use only LEFT JOIN. It makes the intent clearer.

slides.title: LEFT/RIGHT JOIN Practice 🏋️
slides.content:
1. Write a LEFT JOIN to show all customers and their order amounts, ordering by customer name.
2. Write a query to list customers who have no orders.
3. Write a RIGHT JOIN (or swapped LEFT JOIN) to show all orders with customer name, even if customer is missing.

slides.title: Outer Joins Mastered 🎉
slides.content: Now we’ll cover the remaining join types.
